paragraphs: Next it was Achilles’s turn to throw. His spear struck the round shield of Aeneas right at the rim, where the bronze was thinnest, and the Pelian ash shaft went clean through. The shield rang under the blow. Aeneas was afraid. He crouched down and held the shield out away from his body. The spear flew over his back and stuck quivering in the ground, after piercing both rings of the shield that sheltered him. Aeneas had avoided it, but he stood rooted, blinded by fear and grief, because the weapon had come so close. Then Achilles sprang at him in fury, with a deadly cry and his sharp sword drawn. Aeneas picked up a great stone, so huge that two men of today could not have lifted it, though Aeneas swung it easily by himself.

Aeneas would have hit Achilles with that stone as he rushed in, on the helmet or on the shield that covered him, and Achilles would have closed with him and finished him with his sword. But Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, saw it quickly and at once spoke to the immortals. “Alas, I am sorry for great Aeneas. He will soon go down to the house of Hades, beaten by the son of Peleus, because he was a fool to listen to the counsel of Apollo. Apollo will never save him from destruction. Why should this man suffer for nothing, though he is guiltless, in a quarrel that is not his? He has always offered pleasing sacrifices to the gods who live in heaven. Let us snatch him from the jaws of death, in case the son of Cronus is angry if Achilles kills him. Besides, it is fated that he escape, so that the race of Dardanus does not perish utterly, without seed or sign. Zeus loved Dardanus above all the sons born to him of mortal women. Zeus has now come to hate the blood of Priam, so Aeneas shall reign over the Trojans, he and his children’s children who will be born after him.”

Hera answered, “Earth-shaker, decide this matter yourself. Consider whether to save Aeneas, or to let him fall, brave as he is, at the hands of Achilles son of Peleus. Pallas Athena and I have sworn many times before all the immortals that we would never protect the Trojans from destruction, not even when all Troy is burning in the fire the Achaeans will light.”

When earth-encircling Poseidon heard this, he went into the battle through the clash of spears and reached the place where Achilles and Aeneas were. At once he poured a darkness over the eyes of the son of Peleus. He pulled the bronze-headed ash spear out of the shield of Aeneas and laid it at the feet of Achilles. Then he lifted Aeneas high off the ground and hurried him away. Aeneas soared over the heads of many ranks of warriors, both horse and foot, speeding along on the god’s hand, until he reached the far edge of the battle, where the Cauconians were arming for the fight. Poseidon, shaker of the earth, came up to him there and said, “Aeneas, what god has pushed you into this folly of fighting the son of Peleus? He is a mightier man of valor than you, and dearer to heaven. Give way to him whenever you meet him, or you will go down to the house of Hades even though fate wills otherwise. But once Achilles is dead, you can fight among the foremost without fear, for no other Achaean will kill you.”

When the god had given these instructions he left him, and at once lifted the darkness from the eyes of Achilles. Achilles opened them wide and said in great anger, “Alas! What marvel is this I see? My spear lies here on the ground, but I cannot see the man I meant to kill when I threw it. So Aeneas also must be under heaven’s protection, though I thought his boasting was empty. Let him go hang. After so narrow an escape from being killed, he will not want to fight me again. Now I will give my orders to the Danaans and attack some other Trojans.”

He sprang forward along the line and urged his men on. “Do not let the Trojans keep you at arm’s length, Achaeans,” he cried. “Go at them and fight them man against man. However valiant I am, I cannot chase so many and fight them all. Even Ares, who is immortal, or Athena would shrink from plunging into the jaws of such a fight and laying about them. Still, as far as I am able, I will show no slackness of hand or foot and no lack of endurance, not for a moment. I will break their ranks completely, and woe to any Trojan who comes within reach of my spear.”

So he urged them on. Meanwhile Hector called to the Trojans and declared that he would fight Achilles. “Do not be afraid, proud Trojans, to face the son of Peleus,” he said. “I could fight gods myself if the battle were only a matter of words, but they would be too strong for me if we had to use spears. It will be the same with Achilles: his deeds will fall somewhat short of his word. He will do part of it, and the rest he will cut short. I will go up against him even if his hands are like fire—even if his hands are fire and his strength is iron.”

Urged on like this, the Trojans raised their spears against the Achaeans and gave the cry of battle as they threw themselves into the middle of their ranks. But Phoebus Apollo came up to Hector and said, “Hector, you must not challenge Achilles to single combat. Watch for him while you stay under cover of the others, away from the thick of the fight. Otherwise he will hit you with a spear or cut you down at close quarters.”

So he spoke, and Hector drew back into the crowd, afraid at what the god had said to him. Achilles then sprang on the Trojans with a terrible cry, clothed in valor as with a garment. First he killed Iphition son of Otrynteus, a leader of many people. A naiad nymph had borne him to Otrynteus, waster of cities, in the land of Hyde under the snowy heights of Mt. Tmolus. Achilles struck him full on the head as he came at him and split it clean in two. Iphition fell heavily to the ground, and Achilles boasted over him: “You lie low, son of Otrynteus, mighty hero. Your death is here, but your lineage is by the Gygaean lake, where your father’s estate lies, by the fish-rich Hyllus and the eddying waters of Hermus.”

So he boasted, but darkness closed Iphition’s eyes. The chariots of the Achaeans cut him to pieces as their wheels passed over him in the front of the battle. After him Achilles killed Demoleon, a valiant man of war and son of Antenor, striking him on the temple through his bronze-cheeked helmet. The helmet did not stop the spear. It drove on through, crushing the bone, so that the brain inside was scattered in all directions, and his lust for fighting was over. Then Achilles struck Hippodamas in the midriff as he leaped down from his chariot in front of him and tried to escape. Hippodamas breathed his last, bellowing as a bull bellows when young men drag him to be sacrificed to the King of Helice, and the earth-shaker’s heart is glad. Just so he bellowed as he lay dying. Achilles next went after Polydorus son of Priam. His father had always forbidden him to fight, because he was the youngest of his sons, the one Priam loved best, and the fastest runner. In his folly, showing off how swift his feet were, Polydorus was rushing about among the front ranks until he lost his life. Achilles struck him in the middle of the back as he darted past, just where the golden fastenings of his belt were and the two plates of the double breastplate overlapped. The spear point pierced him through and came out by the navel. He fell groaning to his knees, and a cloud of darkness overshadowed him as he sank down holding his entrails in his hands.

When Hector saw his brother Polydorus sinking to the ground with his entrails in his hands, a mist came over his eyes. He could no longer bear to keep his distance. He poised his spear and charged at Achilles like a flame of fire. Achilles saw him and bounded forward, boasting, “Here is the man who has wounded my heart most deeply and killed my beloved comrade. We two will not cower before each other much longer on the highways of war.”

Achilles looked fiercely at Hector and said, “Come closer, so that you meet your doom the sooner.” Hector was not afraid of him and answered, “Son of Peleus, do not think your words can frighten me as if I were a child. I too can brag and talk rudely when I choose. I know you are a mighty warrior, far mightier than I. Nevertheless the outcome lies in the lap of heaven, and worse man though I am, I may yet kill you with my spear, for it too has proved sharp before now.”

He hurled his spear as he spoke, but Athena breathed on it. Though she breathed very lightly, she turned it back away from Achilles, so that it returned to Hector and lay at his feet in front of him. Achilles sprang at him furiously with a loud cry, bent on killing him, but Apollo snatched Hector away easily, as a god can, and hid him in a thick darkness. Three times Achilles sprang at him with spear in hand, and three times he wasted his blow on the air. When he rushed forward a fourth time like a god, he shouted aloud, “Hound, you have escaped death again, though it came very near you this time. Phoebus Apollo, to whom you seem to pray before you go into battle, has saved you once more. But if I too have any friend among the gods, I will surely make an end of you when I meet you another time. For now I will chase down other Trojans.”

Then he struck Dryops with his spear in the middle of the neck, and Dryops fell headlong at his feet. Achilles left him lying there and stopped Demouchus son of Philetor, a brave man of great stature, by hitting him in the knee with a spear. Then he struck him with his sword and killed him. After this he sprang on Laogonus and Dardanus, sons of Bias, and threw them from their chariot, one with a blow from a thrown spear, the other cut down in hand-to-hand fighting. There was also Tros the son of Alastor. He came up to Achilles and clasped his knees, hoping that Achilles would spare him and let him go rather than kill him, because they were the same age. The fool might have known he would not prevail, for Achilles was in no mood for pity or mercy but in grim earnest. So when Tros took hold of his knees and tried to get a hearing for his prayers, Achilles drove his sword into his liver. The liver came rolling out, and Tros’s chest was covered with the black blood that welled from the wound. So death closed his eyes as he lay lifeless.

Achilles next went up to Mulius and struck him on the ear with a spear, and the bronze spearhead came out at the other ear. He struck Echeclus son of Agenor on the head with his sword, and the blade grew warm with blood, while death and stern fate closed the eyes of Echeclus. Next in order the bronze point of his spear wounded Deucalion in the forearm, where the sinews of the elbow join. Deucalion waited for the attack of Achilles with his arm hanging down and death staring him in the face. Achilles cut off his head with a sword blow and flung it, helmet and all, away from him, and the marrow came oozing out of the backbone as Deucalion lay there. Then he went after Rhigmus, noble son of Peires, who had come from fertile Thrace. He struck him through the middle with a spear that lodged in his belly, and Rhigmus fell headlong from his chariot. He also speared Areithous, the squire of Rhigmus, in the back as he was turning his horses to flee, and thrust him from his chariot, while the horses panicked.

Like a fire raging in a mountain glen after long drought, when the dense forest is ablaze and the wind carries great tongues of flame in every direction—so furiously did Achilles rage, wielding his spear like a god and chasing those he meant to kill, until the dark earth ran with blood. Or like a man who yokes broad-browed oxen to tread barley on a threshing floor, and it is soon crushed small under the feet of the lowing cattle—so the horses of Achilles trampled the shields and bodies of the slain. The axle underneath and the railing around the car were spattered with clots of blood thrown up by the horses’ hoofs and by the rims of the wheels. But the son of Peleus pressed on to win still more glory, and his hands were smeared with gore.
